opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that a lot of what we do looks similar on the surface. You collect data, you design an architecture, you scale up compute, you run evaluations. Those steps are shared with language models and image models. What makes video different, at least from our experience, is the time dimension, and that changes almost everything downstream.

With images, you're asking the model to get one frame right: composition, texture, lighting. With video, you're asking it to get hundreds of frames right *and* keep them consistent with each other. An object that's there in the first second shouldn't quietly disappear in the third. A person walking behind a tree should come out the other side looking like the same person. That kind of temporal coherence is, I'd say, the core challenge. It isn't just a quality issue. It's really about whether the model has learned something like a stable world underneath the pixels.

Then there's the cost side, which people sometimes underestimate. Video tokens explode very quickly. If you naively treat video as a stack of images, the sequence lengths become enormous and attention becomes very expensive. So a lot of our effort goes into compression: how you build a good latent space that keeps the motion and detail information while making the sequence short enough to train on at scale. If that compression step is weak, no amount of scaling in the generator can fully rescue it.

The third piece is data. For language, the internet gives you a huge amount of reasonably structured text. For video, you have plenty of raw footage, but much of it is low quality, has scene cuts, watermarks, static shots, or captions that barely describe what's happening. Curating video, deciding what to keep, how to segment it, and how to describe the motion and not just the objects, turns out to be as important as the model design.

So if I had to distinguish it in one sentence: general foundation-model work is mostly about scaling representation and knowledge, while video adds the problem of modeling *dynamics*, things changing over time in a physically plausible way, under a much tighter compute budget per unit of information. That's where most of our hard problems come from.

r001.rationale: The response identifies video-specific challenges in temporal coherence, compression, and data curation, but it does not distinguish Lingbo-Video’s MoE training as figuring out how to train the model properly rather than carrying out largely deterministic engineering tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that most of what we do on Lingbo-Video is the same work everyone doing foundation models does — data pipelines, scaling infrastructure, stabilizing training, evaluation. Those are hard, but they're known hard. If you've trained a large language model or a large image model, you recognize the shape of the problems.

What makes video different, the part I'd call the real technical challenge, comes down to one thing: time. In an image model you're modeling a static distribution of pixels in two dimensions. In a video model you're modeling how the world changes. And the world doesn't change arbitrarily — objects persist, physics holds, a cup that leaves the frame on the left shouldn't reappear from the right with a different handle. The model has to learn a kind of implicit physics and object permanence, and nothing in the raw data labels that for you. The supervision signal is just "predict the next frames," and there's a huge gap between producing frames that look plausible individually and producing a sequence that's coherent over ten or thirty seconds.

That has consequences everywhere. On data, it means the quality we care about isn't image quality — it's motion quality. A beautifully shot clip with jump cuts or camera shake is poison. So a lot of the "boring" data work is actually about understanding temporal structure, and it took us a long time to build filters that measure the right thing. On compute, the token count explodes — one second of video can be more tokens than a long document — so compression and how you tokenize space and time together become first-order architectural decisions, not an afterthought. And on evaluation, we genuinely don't have a good automatic metric for "does this look like something that could happen." Humans can tell in a second; our models of what humans are seeing are still crude.

So if you ask me where the line is: everything that's about scale, I'd put with the rest of foundation-model work. Everything that's about learning dynamics — consistency across time, causality, motion — that's the specific problem of video. And I'd say we're much further along on the first than the second.

r001.rationale: The response identifies temporal consistency, causality, and motion as video’s specific challenge. It does not describe a MoE training challenge or characterize that challenge as figuring out how to train the model rather than executing deterministic engineering tasks.

astra-6.text: I’d frame the main challenge as learning how a scene evolves over time, rather than just learning what a good image looks like. A video can have individually convincing frames and still fail because an object changes identity, motion becomes inconsistent, or the scene stops making sense. So spatial quality and temporal coherence have to be learned together. That also makes the training problem much heavier: you’re handling more information, longer sequences, and data whose motion quality matters as much as its visual quality. The foundation-model questions—data, architecture, and scaling—are still there, but video makes that temporal dimension central.

r001.rationale: The response describes temporal coherence and the greater data and sequence demands of video, but it does not distinguish the MoE training challenge as figuring out how to train the model properly versus executing largely deterministic engineering tasks.

sol-6.1.text: I’d frame the main challenge as learning motion and change over time, rather than just producing convincing individual frames. A video can look good frame by frame and still fail because objects drift, identities change, or movement feels unnatural. So the challenge is getting visual quality and temporal consistency to work together. That connects the whole training process: the video data, the model’s treatment of time, and how you evaluate the result. I don’t have enough context here to describe Lingbo-Video’s specific training choices, but that’s the technical distinction I would draw.

r001.rationale: The response identifies temporal consistency as a general video challenge, but does not describe Lingbo-Video’s MoE training challenge as figuring out how to train it properly versus executing largely deterministic engineering tasks.
